summary: John Henry Wright was a historian, archaeologist, and linguist. He studied at Dartmouth College and the University of Leipzig under Georg Curtius, later teaching at Ohio State, Dartmouth, Johns Hopkins (1886), Harvard (circa 1887–1908), and Athens (1906–1907).

John Herbert Harington was an Indologist and historian. He served at The Asiatic Society as secretary in 1790 and president from 1825 to 1828, and was President of the Council of Fort William College from circa 1801 to 1823.

John Hick worked in philosophy and religious studies. He held posts at Cornell, Princeton Theological Seminary, Cambridge, Birmingham, and Claremont Graduate University, where he served as Danforth Professor (attested 1985–1989).
John Hope studied at the University of Edinburgh from circa 1740 to 1750. He later served on the faculty at the University of Edinburgh from circa 1761 until 1786.

Crook was a scholar of Tibetology and Buddhist studies. He studied at Southampton, Cambridge under Robert Hinde and William Homan Thorpe, and under Sheng Yen. He taught at the University of Bristol (circa 1963–1989) and founded the Western Chan Fellowship.

John Irwin worked in archaeology, Indology, and Buddhist studies. He served as Assistant Keeper (1945) and Keeper (1959–1978) at the Victoria and Albert Museum, and was a visiting professor at the University of Michigan in 1985.

John J. Holder works in philosophy and Buddhist studies. Having studied under Harry Krebs, he held a visiting research post at Oxford and taught philosophy at St. Norbert College, where he was an associate professor by 2018.

Makransky works in Buddhist studies, Tibetology, and philosophy. He earned his PhD at UW–Madison and studied under Lobsang Tendzin and Geshe Lhundup Sopa. In 1992, he joined Boston College as assistant professor of comparative theology and Buddhist studies.

John James Jones was a scholar of Indology and Buddhist studies who completed an M.A. at Aberystwyth University (1911–1914). He served as Assistant Keeper (1926) and Deputy-Keeper (1928) at the National Library of Wales.

John Jorgensen is a scholar of Buddhist studies, Sinology, and Japanology. He worked as a researcher at the Australian National University, taught Japanese studies at Griffith University, and was a Senior Research Associate at La Trobe University (attested 2019).

John Kieschnick is a scholar of Buddhist studies and Sinology. He held a post at the University of Bristol from circa 2003 to 2011 before joining Stanford University in circa 2011 as Professor of Buddhist Studies.

John Lane Bell is a philosopher who completed his D.Phil. at Oxford (1977–1980). He held posts at the London School of Economics (circa 1968–1989), University of Western Ontario, Cambridge (Professor, 2001), and the National University of Singapore.

John Leyden was a linguist and Indologist who studied at Edinburgh, St Andrews, and under Henry Thomas Colebrooke. He served as Professor of Hindustani at Fort William College (1806) and held secretarial posts at The Asiatic Society (circa 1806–1811).

John Lockwood Kipling was an Indologist and historian. He taught at Sir Jamsetjee Jeejebhoy School of Art (1865), served as Principal of the National College of Arts and Curator of Lahore Museum (1875–1893), and edited The Journal of Indian Art and Industry.

John M. Koller is a scholar of philosophy, Indology, and religious studies. He studied at the East-West Center under Shri Krishna Saksena, Charles Alexander Moore, and George T. Artola, and served as a philosophy professor at Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute.

Rosenfield, a historian of Japanese art and Buddhist studies, earned his Ph.D. at Harvard under Benjamin Rowland. He taught at UCLA and Harvard (1965–1991), also serving as Harvard Art Museums' Curator of Oriental Art.

John Marshall was an archaeologist and Indologist. He studied at Cambridge and the British School at Athens, and under Arthur Evans. He served as Director General of the Archaeological Survey of India (1902–1931) and was a fellow at King's College, Cambridge.

John McKenzie was an Indologist and philosopher who studied at Aberdeen, New College, Edinburgh, and Tübingen. He was Professor (from 1908) and Principal (1921–1944) of Wilson College, Mumbai, and Vice-Chancellor of the University of Mumbai (1931–1933).
John McKerrell was a linguist and Indologist. He was an ex officio member of the College of Fort St. George and served as Translator of Telugu and Kannaḍa for the Madras Civil Service in 1804.

John Morrison was an Indologist and religious studies scholar who held a D.D. from the University of Calcutta. He was Principal of Scottish Church College (1889–1904) and lectured at the University of Glasgow (1904) and University of Edinburgh.
